memory_update.text: Treat AI compute leaders, HBM producers, and optical-module leaders as demand anchors; do not let them dominate the New Hotspots map.

InP substrates and raw indium export-permit gates are high-priority chokepoint nodes for AI optical interconnects, with AXTI, COHR, LITE, and VECO as relevant mapping anchors rather than a completed investment ranking.
Advanced PCB substrate glass / T-glass appears to be a concentrated AI-buildout material node with process-knowledge and customer-qualification barriers.
HBM producers are high-attention and likely already priced as obvious beneficiaries; Layer 2A should focus on probe cards, inspection/metrology, process subsystems, and packaging yield-control tools.
Data-center electrical infrastructure may hide underfollowed bottlenecks in switchgear, grid interconnection, electrical rooms, conduit, enclosures, connectors, cable management, and copper wire.
Sulphur and sulphuric acid are non-AI New Hotspot chokepoints with downstream exposure to copper SX-EW, Indonesian HPAL nickel, fertilizer, industrial acid, and vessel-level trade-route shifts.

China sulphuric acid export ban through August 2026, China indium/InP export controls, AI optical 800G/1.6T ramps, advanced-glass capacity additions in 2026-2027, and data-center power interconnection demand are the main catalyst clusters to monitor.

Need primary-source verification for each company node: latest 10-K/10-Q, earnings-call transcripts, customer concentration, backlog, capacity timing, export-permit status, and revenue mix tied specifically to AI, HBM, optical, power, or sulphur-chain exposure.
Need to verify whether Encore Wire remains an investable public-market candidate because the cached Layer 1 universe flags current public status as a verification item.

Need more source work on distributors, certification labs, trade-route logistics firms, port operators, and inspection/testing providers; these may be hidden bottleneck nodes but are not yet adequately mapped from current evidence.

summary: Initial Layer 2A industry-chain map for the 'New Hotspots' theme. The strongest chokepoint-style nodes from the cached evidence cluster around AI optical interconnect materials and tools, AI server substrate materials, HBM/advanced-packaging second-order suppliers, data-center power/electrical balance-of-system, nuclear fuel as regulated baseload input, and non-AI commodity/logistics shocks such as sulphur/sulphuric acid feeding copper, nickel, and fertilizer chains. This map deliberately avoids letting high-attention mega-cap AI leaders dominate the chain; mega-cap or obvious leaders are treated mainly as demand anchors, while underfollowed bottleneck value may hide in substrates, process equipment, inspection/test, electrical infrastructure, regulated feedstocks, and trade-route/certification gates.

supply_chain_map.node: AI data-center compute demand
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Primary demand driver behind higher bandwidth networking, HBM, advanced packaging, power infrastructure, and optical interconnect expansion. High-attention GPU and cloud leaders should be treated as demand anchors rather than the main bottleneck hunting ground.

supply_chain_map.node: 800G/1.6T optical transceivers and AI optical interconnects
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI clusters increase east-west traffic and pull demand for high-speed optical modules, lasers, and photonic components. Bottleneck value may sit one layer upstream in laser materials, InP wafers, epitaxy tools, and qualification capacity rather than in visible networking leaders.

supply_chain_map.node: Indium phosphide substrates and wafers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: InP is a critical upstream material for lasers and high-speed optical components. Cached evidence indicates export controls, raw indium concentration, permit timing volatility, and wafer price pressure, making this a high-priority chokepoint node.

supply_chain_map.node: Raw indium and China export-permit gate
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Regulatory permission to export indium-related materials can act as a non-obvious supply-chain gate. The bottleneck is not only physical capacity but shipment timing, permit approvals, and geographic dependence.

supply_chain_map.node: InP laser manufacturing equipment
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Second-order equipment such as MOCVD, wafer processing, coatings, and deposition tools may become scarce if optical-component makers expand InP laser capacity. Tool vendors can be overlooked because the market focuses on module and laser brands.

supply_chain_map.node: Optical-component makers and vertically integrated InP capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Downstream optical companies validate demand for InP substrates and tools. Their internal capacity expansion can either confirm tight supply or reduce dependence on external substrate vendors, so this node is a key thesis stress point.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced PCB substrate glass / T-glass
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Advanced glass fiber used in high-performance AI server/networking substrates can be a hidden material bottleneck because qualification, glass chemistry, and weaving tolerances are hard to replicate quickly. Cached evidence points to very high supplier concentration and multi-year capacity expansion.

supply_chain_map.node: HBM producers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: HBM is structurally tight, but the obvious producers are already widely followed. For this layer, they function as demand anchors for less obvious probe, inspection, packaging, materials, and subsystem suppliers.

supply_chain_map.node: HBM and advanced-packaging inspection/metrology
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Higher packaging complexity raises the need for yield inspection, metrology, and defect control. These suppliers may be less visible than memory producers or packaging houses but can sit close to capacity and yield bottlenecks.

supply_chain_map.node: HBM and AI accelerator probe cards / electrical test
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Wafer-level and package-level electrical testing becomes more demanding as HBM stacks and AI accelerators grow more complex. Probe-card and test-interface suppliers may hide bottleneck value through qualification, customization, and lead-time constraints.

supply_chain_map.node: Semiconductor subsystems, lasers, vacuum, and process-control components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Diversified subsystem suppliers can benefit from semiconductor capacity expansion but exposure is often hidden across product lines. This node requires careful evidence checks to separate AI/HBM pull-through from normal semiconductor cyclicality.

supply_chain_map.node: Data-center switchgear, electrical rooms, and grid interconnection equipment
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI campus buildouts can strain electrical distribution, switchgear, and substation capacity. Mid-cap or industrial electrical suppliers may be underfollowed because they are not labeled as AI companies.

supply_chain_map.node: Electrical balance-of-system: conduit, cable management, enclosures, connectors, and raceway
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Large data centers require extensive electrical infrastructure beyond GPUs and servers. Lower-attention building-product and electrical-infrastructure companies may benefit if AI campus construction offsets ordinary construction cyclicality.

supply_chain_map.node: Copper wire and cable
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI data centers and grid upgrades can increase copper wiring demand, but margin exposure depends on copper spreads, pricing power, and construction cycles. This is a second-order node with meaningful evidence gaps.

supply_chain_map.node: Utility grid hardware and distribution infrastructure
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Data-center load growth can require utility distribution upgrades, connectors, substations, and grid-hardening equipment. The bottleneck may appear in backlog, lead times, and utility capex programs rather than in AI company disclosures.

supply_chain_map.node: Nuclear fuel enrichment and HALEU
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: If AI power demand increases interest in reliable baseload energy, nuclear fuel and enrichment can become a regulated bottleneck. Policy funding, licensing, Russian-supply substitution, and customer commitments matter more than simple demand narratives.

supply_chain_map.node: Sulphur and sulphuric acid feedstock
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Sulphuric acid is a critical feedstock for copper SX-EW, Indonesian HPAL nickel, fertilizers, and industrial acid markets. Cached evidence describes simultaneous export bans, route disruptions, and Asian supply deficits, making it a non-AI hotspot with cross-sector consequences.

supply_chain_map.node: Copper SX-EW producers dependent on acid supply
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Copper supply can be constrained by sulphuric acid availability, linking a feedstock disruption to electrification and grid buildout inputs. The hidden bottleneck is acid logistics, not necessarily copper ore.

supply_chain_map.node: Indonesian HPAL nickel plants
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: HPAL nickel operations depend heavily on sulphur or sulphuric acid input and may have limited partial-output flexibility. This creates a chokepoint for battery-material supply chains when sulphur routes are disrupted.

supply_chain_map.node: Fertilizer and industrial acid demand
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Sulphuric acid disruptions can spill into fertilizer and industrial markets, competing with copper and nickel buyers for alternative supply. This creates multi-sector demand collision risk.

supply_chain_map.node: New sulphuric acid trade routes and vessel-level logistics
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: When conventional supply routes break, vessel availability, alternative origins, port constraints, and route economics become bottleneck nodes. Logistics and distributors may hide value or risk outside obvious commodity producers.

supply_chain_map.node: Ports, tariffs, and single-point-of-failure supply-chain mapping
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: The broader 'New Hotspots' theme includes supply-chain heat-map work around ports, tariffs, refineries, single suppliers, and origin concentration. These nodes can create pricing power for niche distributors, inspection providers, inventory managers, or logistics firms.
